item.title: Jensen Huang reportedly weighs comeback as tech execs lobby Nvidia board
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Jensen Huang is considering a return as Nvidia ’s chief executive, days after he resigned over reports that he had affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and a subordinate, the Financial Times reported Sunday. Huang has discussed the possibility with confidants, according to the FT, which cited people familiar with the matter. One ally told the paper they were putting together a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby Nvidia’s board for his return and would try to win support from the White House. The ally said Huang backed the effort. Elon Musk and Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney have backed a public letter calling on Nvidia’s board to “Bring Jensen Back.” On Friday, Nvidia shareholders Brad Gerstner of Altimeter Capital and Gavin Baker of Atreides Management urged the board in an open letter to keep “all options on the table, including the potential return of Jensen Huang.” A spokesperson for Nvidia and a spokesperson for Huang declined to comment to the FT. Huang doesn’t hold a controlling stake in Nvidia and can’t overrule its board. The push runs into opposition from Washington. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a “dramatic shakeup” at Nvidia and urged its board to look outside the company for a new CEO. “I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” Bessent said on Fox News, CNBC reported . He said he wants “answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel,” according to Axios . “If this were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed,” Bessent said. Nvidia has said it complies with U.S. export laws. Bessent has also blamed the Commerce Department, led by Secretary Howard Lutnick, for not restricting Megaspeed, the Singapore-based firm at the center of the scandal. “Treasury, War, USTR and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen,” Bessent told CNBC on Friday. Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, CBS News reported . Nvidia reports quarterly earnings Tuesday, its first since Huang’s resignation. Interim CEO Colette Kress has scheduled a company-wide meeting for Wednesday, CNBC reported . The board said Friday it has not yet hired a search firm or “formally engaged any potential candidates” to replace Huang, according to CNBC . The FT reported Friday that the board had approached Arm CEO Rene Haas. Huang resigned Thursday after revelations that he had extramarital affairs with multiple women, one of whom was an alleged Chinese spy. The company said in a statement that Kress, Nvidia’s executive vice president and chief financial officer, will serve as interim CEO. Harvey C. Jones was appointed chair of the board. Nvidia’s stock plunged 13% at the market open Thursday. The company has lost more than $1.2 trillion in market value since the scandal broke in late October, Axios reported. In its statement, the board thanked Huang for his “immeasurable contributions to the company.” The chipmaker is at the center of the global AI economy and has multiple agreements with the U.S. government. Huang, who founded Nvidia in 1993, led the company through the AI boom that made it one of the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies. Last Sunday, Nvidia’s board of directors said it was launching an investigation into Huang being the target of an alleged Chinese spy, with whom he had an affair. Huang admitted to the affair in an email to Nvidia employees and said he is cooperating with the investigation. Reports have identified Alice Huang (no relation), a former executive at tech firm Megaspeed, as the woman he had the relationship with. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Jensen Huang said in a statement. The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, a married Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, joined the company in 2008. On Thursday, Reuters reported that Huang also had an “intimate relationship” with another Nvidia employee. Reuters did not identify the woman, and Nvidia declined to comment. Rep. Brian Mast, the Republican chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told reporters Thursday that Huang had agreed to testify before Congress after being threatened with a subpoena. House Republicans have asked Huang to sit for a closed-door interview on Dec. 1, CNBC reported . Here’s what we know so far, and why the scandal matters. First, who is Jensen Huang? Jensen Huang founded Nvidia, one of the biggest makers of specialized computer chips in the world. Its chips were first designed for computer graphics, but demand for Nvidia’s hardware has skyrocketed with the AI boom of the past few years. China and the U.S. are in a heated competition for AI technology, and that includes access to chips like the ones Nvidia makes. Huang is an American citizen who was born in Taiwan. He founded Nvidia in 1993 and served as its president and CEO until Thursday. What we know about the Huang affair so far According to the New York Times , it’s unclear when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, but the two were photographed together in 2024 at a bar in Taipei, Taiwan. That was roughly when Megaspeed, the AI company she worked for, began its push into the AI sector. News reports have not confirmed whether Alice Huang still works at Megaspeed. Megaspeed has touted its membership in Nvidia’s partnership program, which would give it access to Nvidia’s latest technology. Huang apologized for the affair in a message to Nvidia employees and asked for privacy for his family. “I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused,” Huang wrote, “and I accept the criticism that comes with it.” He pledged to earn back his employees’ confidence and said he was cooperating fully with the board’s investigation. “I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security,” he wrote. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang was gathering information for the Chinese government. China denied that it was spying , calling the allegation unsubstantiated. “It is nothing but smears against China,” a Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson said. The New York Times also reported that Nvidia executives contacted the U.S. Commerce Department last year seeking information about the department’s investigation into Megaspeed. The investigation was later transferred to the Justice Department, which is reportedly looking into whether Megaspeed illegally routed Nvidia products into China. Why this matters AI is the biggest thing in tech right now, from chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude to software development and bioengineering. Governments are trying to work out how to use AI for security and across the economy, and China and the U.S. are racing to lead its development. The technology has moved so fast that some CEOs of AI companies have suggested a pause before it develops beyond what humans can control. Nvidia has contracts with the U.S. government to use its technology in several areas , and Huang has a close relationship with President Trump. U.S. officials are trying to determine whether the affair allowed the Chinese government to obtain information about Nvidia’s technology and its agreements with the U.S. government. Nvidia’s board said in its statement that it does not believe national security or company secrets were compromised. Trump said last Sunday that he considers Huang “a fine person” who should stay on as CEO of Nvidia. “I think he probably has an excuse for it. We’ll have to hear it,” Trump told reporters. “He’s done an amazing job for our country.” On Tuesday, the New York Times reported that Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also national security adviser, told Trump in May that the U.S. believed Huang was involved with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Trump received the information aboard Air Force One en route to a summit in China, the Times reported. Huang went with the president on that trip. The Times said it was not the first time Trump had been told about U.S. intelligence on the affair. But the president said this week he was not aware of Huang’s affair when Huang joined him for the China summit. item.title: Russian diesel under Trump deal struggles to reach U.S. market amid legal fears and criticism
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A general view shows a refinery in Volgograd, Russia, April 22, 2022. - Reuters/File More than a month after President Donald Trump announced a surprise deal to import Russian diesel , the oil has struggled to reach the US market amid outrage and legal concerns. Several oil tankers that departed from a key Russian oil-loading port — and are believed to be laden with diesel — are no longer bound for the US, according to ship tracking data from MarineTraffic, and US businesses and ports have steered clear of accepting Russian diesel for fear of legal and reputational risks, experts told CNN. Bipartisan lawmakers and European allies expressed outrage at the agreement that Trump said he reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin to bring tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel into US and global markets. They condemned it as a concession to Russia as it continued its war against Ukraine and warned that those who imported the diesel could run afoul of international sanctions and US law. One of the tankers, Agioi Fanendes , departed Russia with tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel. Its destination was listed as the Port of New York and New Jersey, and it was initially expected to arrive around November 7. As of Sunday, the vessel was hovering hundreds of miles off the eastern coast of the US. It was officially broadcasting “FOR ORDERS” instead of a destination port. A spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited, the company that operates the tanker, told CNN on Thursday that its “discharging port is not confirmed yet.” Several other oil tankers that departed Primorsk — one of Russia’s largest oil-loading ports — in mid-October have also shifted away from the US, according to data from MarineTraffic reviewed by CNN. One, the Talisman, docked at the Port of Alexandria in Egypt in recent days. Another, the Leruo, is now heading to Brazil. They had earlier declared their destinations as the US Atlantic coast. Both vessels are under European and British sanctions, and the Talisman is also sanctioned in the US. A White House official told CNN on Wednesday that “consistent with the deal agreed to between President Trump and President Putin, Russian diesel is on the water and heading to the market, which will ease prices for Americans.” The official did not say the diesel was heading to the US. The person said the deal “was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done.” Trump announced in a social media post on October 9 that he had reached a deal with Putin for Russia to “immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace.” The administration billed the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections amid steep fuel costs, as a way to lower prices for US consumers. Experts said the diesel would have little to no impact on prices, and amounts to less than a day of US energy consumption. Questions about legality of importing Russian fuel Last month, a group of bipartisan lawmakers sent letters to the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and the heads of Port Authorities of New York/New Jersey and of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont, Texas, warning that they could face legal action if they are involved in importing the Russian diesel into the US. The Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 bans Russian-origin energy products, including diesel fuel, from being imported into the US “unless — following a period for consultation with Congress — the President certifies to Congress that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, that Russia poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and that Russia recognizes the right of Ukrainians to choose their government,” the lawmakers warned . Although the US Treasury Department issued a sanctions waiver to allow the import of the diesel under the deal between the Trump administration and Moscow, the lawmakers consider that sanctions waiver to defy the law. “Any importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations,” wrote Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons, Elizabeth Warren, GOP Sen. Thom Tillis, and Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks. “Criminal penalties may apply to any company that knowingly buys Russian diesel or facilitates its importation, and not simply the importer of record,” they wrote. New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill warned her state’s port and terminal operators last week that “any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties.” Charles Lichfield, the director of economic foresight and analysis and the C. Boyden Gray senior fellow at the Atlantic Council’s GeoEconomics Center, noted that US importers would face “the immediate reputational risk” as well as the legal ramifications. He noted that a general license from the Treasury Department, which allows businesses to import the diesel without fear of sanctions, would appear to be good protection but the 2022 law is still on the books, which raises questions about legality and the potential for prosecution down the line. “All of this is very politically charged (and) the volumes are small,” he said. “You could make a few million dollars off this shipment, but is it really worth it?” Julian Hayda, the associate director for advocacy at the organization Razom for Ukraine, noted that “now that Democrats have control of both chambers of Congress, they are most certainly going to launch investigations into these companies, so it’s not going to be worth it for many of these companies to buy this vehicle in and when it arrives on American shores.” This story has been updated with additional information. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/15/politics/russia-diesel-trump-deal-oil-tankers

item.title: Trump plan could leave decommissioned oil rigs lying on the seafloor off California
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Offshore oil and gas platform Harvest, in the Point Arguello field of the Santa Maria Basin off the California coast. (Chip Chipman / Bloomberg via Getty Images) A quiet proposal from the Trump administration could change the way offshore oil platforms are managed when they reach the end of their useful lives, leaving more of them to lie permanently on the seafloor off the coast of California. Buried within a September executive order about recreational fishing, President Trump directed the Department of the Interior — through its newly formed Marine Minerals Administration — to establish a federal “reef-in-place” program for decommissioned offshore oil and gas platforms. “Reefing” refers to leaving all or part of the metal structures in the ocean, where they can become artificial reefs for marine life. There are 23 platforms in federal waters off the state’s coast currently, eight of which are in various stages of decommissioning. Four others are within state waters. The Interior Department has signaled that it intends to go one step further. A rulemaking scheduled for 2027 would make “toppling in place” the default decommissioning method if approved. It’s largely what it sounds like: knocking all or most of the platform over onto its side to rest on the sea bottom. Though it’s been done in the Gulf of Mexico, it has never been tried in the Pacific waters off California, where all previously decommissioned platforms have been removed. Read more: Trump wants to strip California of coastal protections unless state yields to list of demands Critics say the action is designed to benefit fossil fuel companies, which have already profited from several sweeping policy changes since the president returned to office last year. Full removal of some of the largest offshore platforms could cost more than $200 million, according to federal estimates. “Decommissioning via topple in place would be a huge windfall for oil companies in comparison to full removal, allowing them to avoid hundreds of millions of dollars in expenses as well as complex engineering and contracting problems,” said Robert Collier, an oil industry consultant who first flagged the plan on his Substack, Offshore California. It comes as the White House seeks to reopen waters in the Pacific to new oil leasing for the first time in more than 40 years, along with new lease areas in Alaska and the Gulf of Mexico. Trump’s executive order specifies that offshore wind platforms would not benefit from the policy change. The president’s opposition to offshore wind is well documented. Regardless of the motivation, some scientists say the change could be a good thing for marine life. While some habitats can be disrupted when the platforms are installed, many fish and other species have come to thrive in and on the metal structures over time, including different types of rockfish, mussels and anemones, according to Milton Love, a research biologist at UC Santa Barbara. For this reason, the question of what to do with an oil platform at the end of its life raises interesting scientific and moral questions, Love said. Removing the structure from the water kills the invertebrate life on it, he said, and crews sometimes use underwater explosives in the process, which can kill nearby fish. “They happen to be living next to a piece of steel, and you’re going to kill them for that? I just don’t think that’s right,” he said. One reefing method is something of a middle ground, and typically involves severing the platform at 85 feet below sea level, where officials say it will no longer pose a threat to ships above. Toppling changes the conditions even more — converting the whole structure to a deep-water habitat. It’s hard to say what that would mean for the platforms off the coast of California, which vary in depth from about 95 to 1,200 feet in federal waters. While hundreds of platforms have been reefed via various methods in the Gulf of Mexico, the scientific findings there aren’t really applicable to the Pacific because of differences in species, water conditions, depths and other factors, Love said. “Putting the platforms in was a great experiment in terms of biology,” he said, “and tipping them over would be a great experiment again.” Read more: Trump administration plans to open Pacific Coast to oil drilling for first time in more than 4 decades Some environmental and coastal advocacy groups strongly oppose any form of reefing or toppling, which they argue lets fossil fuel companies off the hook for their environmental legacy. “What they’re asking for now isn’t even partial decommissioning — it appears to be ocean dumping,” said Richard Charter, director of the Local Government Outer Continental Shelf Coordination Program, a coalition of coastal counties opposed to offshore drilling. Charter said that the plan doesn’t only save the oil industry money on existing platforms, but that it also incentivizes new oil leasing. That’s because some companies are more willing to invest in remote drilling sites if they know they’ll never have to remove their rigs, he said. The federal government is also approaching the issue another way. A bipartisan bill, HR 5745, would make it easier for eligible oil and gas platforms to be converted into reefs via toppling, severing or abandonment. It provides for transferring liability for rigs to states that accept them into their artificial reef programs in exchange for compensation. Reefed rigs can also provide opportunities for fishing and tourism. “Offshore energy infrastructure becomes valuable marine habitat, supporting an abundance of fish and other marine life,” said Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Assn., in an official statement about the legislation. “That is especially important in the Gulf of America, where natural reef habitat is limited,” he said, referring to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump’s preferred name. “Rigs-to-Reefs provides a proven way to preserve that habitat and extend the benefits of offshore infrastructure long after energy production ends,” Milito said. If the plans advance, they are likely to face legal challenges from coastal groups and counties, and possibly the state as well, Charter said. But any challenges could be slowed by a larger fight playing out over California’s coastal authority. The Trump administration is trying to strip the state’s power under the Coastal Zone Management Act, a long-standing law that grants California the right to object to projects in federal waters that clash with state policy. California did establish its own rigs-to-reef program in 2010 under legislation signed by then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger. Platforms may be reefed in place on a case-by-case basis by removing their upper portions, with oil companies sharing some of the cost savings with the state and transferring some of the long-term liability. It does not allow for toppling in place. Nearly two decades later, no platform has yet been reefed under the program. Platform Holly, which sits in state waters off the coast of Goleta, is in the decommissioning process and could be a test of California’s policy, said Linda Krop, chief counsel with the nonprofit Environmental Defense Center. The State Lands Commission is weighing whether to sever or fully remove the platform and is expected to release a draft environmental impact report early next year. Krop suspects the state will favor full removal because it won’t want to manage the platform and be liable for it into the future. Liability questions aside, she said she is also opposed to reefing and toppling for environmental reasons, including concerns about invasive species and contamination from heavy metals. “We’re very concerned about leaving this legacy pollution” in the ocean, she said. “If it was onshore, you know no one would allow it.” Sign up for Boiling Point, our twice-weekly newsletter on energy, the environment and climate across the American West. This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times . This article originally appeared on LA Times at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/offshore-oil-rigs-could-toppled-110000945.html

item.title: Parents whose sons died from kratom use offer warnings as the drug remains legal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Kratom, a substance that acts on opioid receptors, can be as easy to obtain as a bag of chips. Kratom is derived from a tree native to Southeast Asia, where for generations people have chewed the leaves or boiled them to make a stimulating tea with opioid effects. The sales of kratom in the U.S. have fueled a billion-dollar industry, with products containing the plant available online and in tens of thousands of stores across the country, including gas stations. The kratom industry hails the substance as a mild stimulant that can also aid in recovery from opioid addiction. The kratom industry has supporters in the highest ranks of government and is legally sold in most states. But health experts warn that kratom use can lead to addiction and death. Dr. Andrew Kolodny, the medical director for the Opioid Policy Research Collaborative at Brandeis University, said that it has effects very similar to those of oxycodone, heroin and even fentanyl. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has detected kratom in more than 5,000 overdose deaths from 2020-2024. Helping shape perception of kratom as a benign health supplement is the consumer advocacy and lobby group the American Kratom Association. The group describes natural kratom as "a safe food used by many as an herbal supplement" taken for "health and wellbeing or for an energy boost." Four families told "60 Minutes" that their sons, all recently deceased, started using kratom for those kinds of benefits. Susan Eppard's son Matthew told her it was like coffee, because he read it was related to the coffee family. Patti Wheeler's son Wyatt said it was helping him ease away from alcohol. "He was looking for something for energy. A friend of his told him it was safer than Red Bull," said Wendy Chamberlain about her son Joe. The deaths of Matthew and Joe were attributed solely to mitragynine, the main opioid in kratom. Daniel Bregger and Wyatt Wheeler's causes of death included mitragynine along with prescription or over-the-counter medications. Susan Eppard said her son collapsed suddenly while playing cards with friends. She recalled the day her son died. "They tried resuscitating him for a long time. [By the] time I got there, they wouldn't let me in at first, so I'd just sit out on the ground outside screaming for God to keep my baby here," Susan Eppard said. "And they finally let me go in there and see him. I knelt down to him and gave him a kiss on his forehead. And he was just cold and dark and gray." Justin Brower, a toxicologist at NMS Labs, a forensic testing facility 40 minutes outside Philadelphia, said he has analyzed thousands of deaths involving kratom. "Dozens and dozens" have been attributed "just to kratom, no other drugs at all," he said. Fatalities linked to kratom have "increased probably about tenfold" since 2014, he said. "It's pretty incredible how it's taken hold of the United States and how many people are using it now, compared to, you know, a decade-plus ago," Brower said. The Food and Drug Administration warns "consumers not to use kratom because of the risk of serious adverse events, including liver toxicity, seizures, and substance use disorder." With concern growing over kratom-derived products, including the concentrated kratom-related synthetic substance 7-OH, the federal government announced in July that it would restrict 7-OH and three related substances found in kratom products. But then last month, the Department of Health and Human Services changed its recommendation . Among the new recommendations: increasing the amount of 7-OH allowed in products by 20-fold. Some health officials, including former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary and former senior HHS advisor Calley Means, were stunned by the decision. "60 Minutes" found public filings from the last decade that show a constant stream of cash -- much from the American Kratom Association — earmarked for lobbying the FDA, HHS, the White House, and members of Congress. Millions of dollars committed to keeping kratom legal. Even more money has come in the form of political contributions and investments. Kolodny compared it to the lobbying actions of Purdue Pharma, the manufacturer of OxyContin. "Some of the same scientists who Purdue Pharma hired to make sure that regulators wouldn't take action against OxyContin are now working for the Kratom Association and delivering the same message, downplaying the risks, exaggerating the numbers of people who are potentially benefiting," Kolodny said. HHS declined an interview request with "60 Minutes," but said in a statement that "Neither political contributions nor outside pressure influenced" the decision to increase the amount of 7-OH allowed in products. The American Kratom Association gave a statement to "60 Minutes" and emphasized the distinction between natural kratom and "dangerous chemically manipulated products." Eppard said she can't believe that kratom, in any form, is still for sale. She said she often goes into convenience stores to ask employees if they realize what they are selling. Often, they don't, she said. So she tells them about her son. "We all just miss him terrible," she told "60 Minutes." This article originally appeared on CBS News at https://www.cbsnews.com/news/parents-whose-sons-died-from-kratom-use-warn-about-substance-60-minutes/

item.title: Bill Cassidy, both a doctor and senator, calls for Trump to replace Kennedy at HHS
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., speaks to members of the media on April 29, 2021, in Washington, D.C. (Stefani Reynolds/Getty Images) Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., called Sunday for President Donald Trump to replace Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., saying his handling of measles, rising healthcare costs, and ultraprocessed foods amounts to a series of failures. "If I were president, I would choose someone else because there needs to be accountability for higher healthcare costs, more measles deaths, losing elimination status, and no progress on processed foods," Cassidy told CBS' "Face the Nation." Cassidy, a physician who chairs the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, said Kennedy's record could damage Trump's legacy unless the president changes course. "The American voters signaled at the midterm they don't like status quo, particularly in healthcare. And I think it's time for something different," he said. His criticism followed a recording played during the interview in which Kennedy said the Senate would no longer have leverage over him after Democrats take control in January. "The Senate no longer has any leverage over me and, you know, that's a big deal," Kennedy said. "Then we have [Trump chief of staff] Steve Miller, who is a friend of our movement, and I don't think anything is going to get in our way now." Cassidy dismissed that reasoning, saying Kennedy was "obviously trying to provide cover for failure as secretary of health and human services." He said mothers who supported Kennedy had expected action on ultraprocessed foods but had seen minimal progress. Hundreds contacted Cassidy during the debate over whether he should support Kennedy's confirmation, he said. "They have every right to be disappointed," Cassidy said. He also pointed to small businesses dropping health coverage and employees struggling to afford deductibles. "This has been a failure," he said. Asked whether Kennedy should face impeachment, Cassidy emphasized Trump's responsibility for deciding whether to keep him. "As regards impeachment, you know, you can impeach, I guess, over a ham sandwich. They will have to decide what to do on that," he said. "I do think it's more importantly the president's decision." Cassidy also called for stronger public messaging about vaccination after host Margaret Brennan cited reporting that the United States had lost its measles elimination status. He warned that people who choose not to get vaccinated can expose infants too young to receive the vaccine and people with weakened immune systems to measles. "If you have not been vaccinated, you could be the person that brings death to another," Cassidy said. "That's something to remember." He said the administration should repeatedly emphasize those risks. "I think that should be the message going out. It should be pounded, pounded, pounded," he said. Cassidy said he remains in regular contact with the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but the limited time remaining before the end of the congressional session could complicate scheduling a public hearing. He cited his recent exchange with the director about a broken online tool for locating flu shots as an example of oversight taking place outside hearings. Cassidy also declined to predict whether his committee would advance the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton, Trump's choice to lead the Food and Drug Administration, in a vote scheduled for Wednesday. Trump nominated Overton in September. "I've been working the phones all week. Speaking with Overton, speaking with others, I still have questions," he said. Brennan noted Cassidy had previously described Overton's role in developing the administration's childhood vaccine policies as almost disqualifying. Cassidy said senators must weigh their concerns against the possibility of leaving the FDA under a succession of temporary leaders who could be more susceptible to Kennedy's influence. A permanent commissioner could establish greater independence, he said. "It continues to be back and forth, and we will know Wednesday," Cassidy said. On Social Security, Cassidy expressed frustration over the prospects for advancing legislation before year's end, accusing Senate Finance Committee ranking member Ron Wyden, D-Ore., of resisting a hearing. Cassidy said Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Finance Committee Chair Mike Crapo, R-Idaho, had committed to a hearing and committee vote on a Social Security bill. Trump also had personally committed his support, Cassidy said. His proposal would borrow $1.5 trillion to establish an investment fund separate from the Social Security trust fund, allowing the money to grow over six decades to help address the program's long-term financing needs. Cassidy said Wyden opposes investing taxpayer money in the stock market but contended that a similar approach had succeeded for the federal railroad retirement system. He said he was willing to consider other proposals, including one from Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt. "Congress is there to take tough choices, and now those tough choices are being ducked," Cassidy said. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved.This article originally appeared on Newsmax at https://www.newsmax.com/newsfront/bill-cassidy-rfk-jr-hhs/2026/11/15/id/1276363

item.title: Army whistleblower says warnings went ignored before 6 U.S. troops were killed in Kuwait
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
A U.S. Army soldier who survived a deadly Iranian drone attack filed a whistleblower complaint to Congress alleging senior military officials ignored warnings and did not plan properly for anti-drone defenses ahead of the war with Iran . The whistleblower, Army Maj. Stephen Ramsbottom, spoke exclusively with 60 Minutes' Norah O'Donnell about his complaint, which was submitted to the House and Senate Armed Services Committees on Friday and obtained by CBS News. He alleges Army leaders dismissed concerns over thin fortifications at a U.S. command post in Kuwait where six American soldiers were killed by an Iranian drone in the first 24 hours of the conflict, the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war. The complaint also claims the post — known as Port Shuaiba — "had no physician, no fixed aid station, and only one ambulance." "I feel this is a tactical failure by the Army, our leadership, and myself — all the way down to my level," Maj. Ramsbottom told 60 Minutes. "We just did not plan this well, and this needs to be a lesson that we learn." Ramsbottom spoke with 60 Minutes as part of an eight-month investigation into the March 1 attack at the command post, known as Port Shuaiba. The day after the attack, in a press conference, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth insisted the troops there were well protected. "Every once in a while you might have one, unfortunately, we call it a squirter that makes its way through," Hegseth said. "And in that particular case it happened to hit a tactical operations center that was fortified. But these are powerful weapons." The eyewitness accounts, along with photos and videos of the attack's aftermath, offer a staggering look at the thinly fortified Kuwaiti port facility when it was hit one day after the U.S. and Israel launched Operation Epic Fury. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat from Connecticut and the ranking member on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, issued a series of demands to Hegseth after reviewing the whistleblower complaint. In a letter dated Nov. 15, the senator called on Hegseth to appear in a classified briefing and provide "all force protection assessments" for Port Shuaiba. Democrats have signaled they will probe the administration's handling of the war with Iran when they retake both houses of Congress next year. "The families of the six fallen servicemembers, the wounded survivors, and the American people deserve transparency and accountability," wrote Blumenthal. A Pentagon spokesperson declined to comment on Ramsbottom's allegations, including on whether adequate force protection was in place at Port Shuaiba. item.title: Founder of notorious Guadalajara cartel, imprisoned since 1989, dies at 80
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Diego Oré and Michelle Freyria MEXICO CITY/GUADALAJARA, Nov 15 (Reuters) - Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, founder of one of Mexico's first major drug cartels whose conviction for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement ‌agent made him one of the country's most notorious traffickers, died in hospital on Sunday at age 80. Local ‌security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ ​failure and died around 2 p.m. on Sunday. Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was an inmate in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health. Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico's modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led ‌to hundreds of thousands of deaths and ⁠disappearances in ensuing decades. Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and bodyguard for a local governor ⁠then became a powerful criminal capo known as the "boss of bosses." Felix Gallardo and others set up the cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and ​to forge ​an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar's Medellin ​cartel. His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and ‌1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials and innovations like using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero. His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug-trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel. While already incarcerated, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration agent Enrique "Kiki" Camarena and Mexican pilot ‌Alfredo Zavala Avelar. Camarena's killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressed ​Mexico hard to arrest those involved. In 2017, a federal court found Felix ​Gallardo guilty in that case and imposed a ​further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings. His rise and fall was portrayed on screen ‌by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 ​hit Netflix series "Narcos: Mexico". Felix Gallardo ​suffered poor health in his final years, and was blind in one eye, practically deaf and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained ​his innocence. "Thirty-two years have passed... That's ‌an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime," he said. (Reporting by Jose Gonzalez in ​Ciudad Juarez and Diego Ore, Noe Torres and Sarah Morland in Mexico City; Additional reporting by Raul ​Cortes; Editing by Rosalba O'Brien, Edmund Klamann and Cynthia Osterman) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/mexicos-guadalajara-cartel-founder-aged-213009881.html

item.title: Trump's handpicked party chair faces a rebellion in wake of midterm losses
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — A nascent rebellion is underway against President Donald Trump's handpicked chairman at the Republican National Committee, and it’s already getting ugly. Some members are calling for a forensic audit of spending decisions, including hair and makeup services for Trump and other officials, as well as the hiring of the daughter of Trump's former chief of staff. Feuding Republicans are leaking emails and opposition research on rival factions. The White House is threatening to cut off fundraising assistance if the rebels don’t fall in line. The emerging fight, which will shape the 2028 presidential nominating contest, represents a rare challenge to Trump's dominance, even after the party's worst midterm performance in a generation. Despite the broad losses, Republican leaders across Washington have shown little desire to move past Trump and have largely stood behind his most unpopular policies. But inside the Republican National Committee, an organization of 168 members elected from every state who oversee the party’s national political operation, a small and growing collection of concerned Republicans are backing an attempt to depose Joe Gruters. Trump wants to keep him in charge. The dissidents are rallying behind Kentucky’s KC Crosbie, the RNC's second-in-command. She launched her bid just two days after the Nov. 3 election in a letter that drew the fury of both the White House and Gruters' allies. Crosbie remains a vocal Trump supporter who backs his “Make America Great Again” agenda, but her opponents view her gambit as a direct challenge to the president and his power. “Our job is to elect Republicans broadly, not to support one man all the time," said RNC member Oscar Brock of Tennessee, who is supporting Crosbie’s candidacy. He said that requires a change in leadership because “there’s so much frustration that Chairman Gruters didn’t pull his weight in this election.” In her letter, Crosbie described the midterms as “a serious setback" and called for the RNC to provide “an honest account” of what went wrong. Crosbie declined to be interviewed. The leadership election will be held in January at the RNC’s winter meeting in Arizona. Inside the rebellion against Gruters Some would-be Crosbie supporters privately acknowledge they're worried about a backlash from the White House, especially with Stephen Miller taking over as Trump's chief of staff. Others believe in the committee's tradition of having presidents pick their own party chiefs. Gruters also has vocal backers. Lauren LePage, an RNC member from Maine, praised Gruters' leadership and efforts to help her father, Paul LePage, flip a congressional seat — a rare bright spot for Republicans this cycle. “From my perspective, as chairman, he did his job," she said, adding that Trump's endorsement is “something that the committee should take very seriously.” The Republicans who have lined up behind Crosbie insist a leadership change is needed to send a clear message that the party will do things differently after losses even in Republican strongholds like Texas , South Carolina and Mississippi . Patti Lyman, an RNC member from Virginia, said it would be “catastrophic” and “insulting” to the party’s base “to keep the same leadership and pretend that we don’t need to do anything different, that we don’t need new players and a new plan.” Sue Cienki, an RNC committee member from Rhode Island, predicted that Crosbie would have the backing of at least two members from 10 states — a total of 20 — at the committee's January meeting. That's the minimum required for a successful nomination. Trump is furious with Crosbie Trump and senior White House officials were livid about Crosbie’s Nov. 5 letter and the fact that they were given no heads-up. The president soon released a lengthy statement on his Truth Social social media platform hailing Gruters as a “MAGA Warrior” and giving him his “Complete and Total Endorsement.” Trump is expected to play a central role in picking the party's next presidential nominee. The party's future is at stake Allies of Gruters say a leadership change now would put the RNC at a severe disadvantage heading into the next presidential cycle because a new team would need time to get up to speed. They say friction between the president and the committee's leadership would curtail their ability to organize and raise money. They also reject Crosbie's call for a postelection review, which they said would do little more than consume six months rehashing the past and put all their grievances on paper. Gruters spent much of this week holding private phone conversations with committee members. Those who participated in the calls said Gruters listened to their grievances, but said little about what he would do differently. Spending faces scrutiny The opposition to Gruters has focused on the RNC's spending decisions under him. Republicans had a massive fundraising advantage and still had deep losses. “There’s clearly a groundswell of support for a forensic audit,” said Brock, the RNC member from Tennessee. In a letter to RNC members sent Thursday night and obtained by The Associated Press, Gruters acknowledged concerns about spending and other issues. Gruters defended a $22,500 expenditure for hospitality space at the Presidents Cup, a golf event, saying the space was offered to major donors and "resulted in $2.5 million in renewed contributions to the RNC.” He also addressed “a brief contract” between the RNC and Caroline Wiles, a longtime Republican consultant, who is the daughter of Susie Wiles, Trump's former chief of staff. Gruters said she was hired by his predecessor at the committee, Michael Whatley. “While I have no reason to doubt Caroline Wiles’s value to the RNC or Chairman Whatley’s reasons for bringing her on, this was a brief six-month engagement that ended when I was elected Chairman,” he wrote. Gruters also defended the RNC's decision to pay for “hair and make-up services” for senior White House officials, including Trump, Vice President JD Vance and former press secretary Karoline Leavitt. “This was a request made of us so that the expense did not fall to taxpayers,” Gruters wrote, adding that the beneficiaries “generously gave so much of their limited time and energies to help the RNC this cycle” and “did not ask for much of us in return, so we felt this was a request we could accommodate.” This article originally appeared on Associated Press at https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/trumps-handpicked-party-chair-faces-192048723.html

item.title: A viral ad helped flip a Senate seat in Mississippi. Its star expected just 100 views.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Russ Hudson appears in a campaign ad for Scott Colom. - From Scott Colom for Senate Russ Hudson of Columbus, Mississippi, became one of the unexpected stars of the 2026 midterms, with a feature role in an ad that’s since been viewed more than 20 million times on X alone – tipping his head back and exclaiming, “sheeeit.” “It’s been crazy. Like, I never expected it to do this,” Hudson told CNN in an interview, reflecting on the ad for Democratic Sen.-elect Scott Colom that helped spark one of the biggest political upsets of the election cycle. Posted to social media on October 13, the ad features Hudson and other Mississippians rebuking incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for suggesting there are many other proteins to chose from when pressed on high beef prices. “Pick another protein, sheeeit,” Hudson says in the spot as he grills burgers. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.” “When I originally told Scott I would do it, I thought maybe like 100, maybe 1,000 views at most,” Hudson said. “I never expected it to do what it did. And I didn’t have TikTok. I literally had to download TikTok to see what all the hype was about because a bunch of my friends were sending messages like, ‘Dude, you’re like worldwide.’” Hudson said that he’d been recognized in public a few times and asked for pictures, “like I’m some superstar or something.” “So it’s a little weird. I’m not used to that, obviously,” he said. Hudson, the father of a four-month-old infant and an Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, said that he’d known Colom for a decade, and that his sister had worked with him. The initial plan called for Hudson’s father to appear in the ad, but he was reluctant to curse on camera, so the younger Russ volunteered. “I just went to his mom’s house in the backyard, and we fired up the grill, and they gave me the lines, and we just rolled with it,” Hudson said. For the signature line – the “s-h-e-e-e-i-t,” as Hudson spells it – he said they did about ten to fifteen takes, but that Colom said he nailed it on the third. “That’s something we say. And my buddy was talking to me on the phone the other day, and he said something. I was like, ‘sheeeit!’ He was like, ‘There you go.’ It’s just a thing, man,” Hudson laughed. Underscoring the ad’s point, Hudson also recalled saving the burgers he’s seen flipping on the grill. “[Colom] told me to save the burgers because beef prices were high. So, I didn’t want to waste them,” Hudson said. Asked what he thought of the comment from Hyde-Smith that started it all, telling Mississippians to pick another protein, Hudson said that “it’s ridiculous.” “We deserve better than that, and that’s why one of the reasons I really wanted to back Scott, you know, because I mean he wants to make things affordable for us here in Mississippi,” Hudson said. Senator-elect Scott Colom raises a fist after speaking during his victory rally at Tougaloo College in Tougaloo, Miss., on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. . - Lauren Witte/Clarion Ledger/USA Today Network/Reuters He also considered the landmark victory, saying that “it’s pretty cool – I know it’s gonna go down in history. My mom keeps reminding me of that, and I’m just like, yeah, it’s pretty cool to be a part of that.” “But the main thing is, is the goal was to help Scott win this election, and it did that,” he said, crediting the advertisement’s writers and producers for “all the work.” As for what he’ll remember from the experience, Hudson paused for a moment. “The Mississippi folks will appreciate this,” Hudson said, before referencing musician Doughbelly Stray. “[He] did a song one time that says, ‘My Mississippi ain’t on this map,’ and our Mississippi’s on this map now. So that’s what I remember from it as we put Mississippi on the map,” he said. Ryan Sayles, the creative mind behind the ad, joined CNN’s “The Arena with Kasie Hunt” on Thursday and shared more details on the production. Saying he wanted to bring a “Mississippi feel to it,” Sayles instructed the individuals reading the lines to “drag it out so people can really feel how you feel.” He also picked the catchy backing track – “Rapper’s Delight” by Sugarhill Gang – crediting his dad’s influence as a former DJ. unknown content item - “I was a class clown, you know. I joke a lot, so I definitely think that this helped people look at it and say, “Oh man, this is funny,” but that’s really how I feel, you know,” Sayles said, underlining the importance of humor in political messaging. “Like it was funny, but it wasn’t funny, you know what I mean? It was a good way to just get attention and bring national attention to Mississippi.” And Sayles praised Colom for his engagement with the process and willingness to take risks, saying that “he thinks about how he can reach people that normally wouldn’t be reached.” Eight days after Election Day, CNN projected that Colom would defeat Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate in Mississippi in more than four decades. The outcome ranks as perhaps the most stunning upset in an election cycle full of historic wins as Democrats capitalized on sharp voter backlash to the Trump administration. In a nod to the viral ad at his victory party last week, Colom stood at a lectern behind a sign that read “picked another senator” as he thanked Mississippians for their support.
